newsitem.title: USA: USDA analysts see Brazil seeking US soybeans soon.
newsitem.headline: USDA analysts see Brazil seeking US soybeans soon.

text.p: Agriculture Department analysts look for Brazil to be in the market very soon for U.S. soybeans in order to replenish currently tight supplies and keep its soybean crushers operating through the winter.

"Brazil could be buying up to 500,000 tonnes or more of U.S. beans over the next few months to crush. They've used up their beans," said Jim Matthews, head of USDA's interagency soybean estimates committee.

Matthews and others said that due to a shorter crop this past year and brisk sales, Brazilian soybean supplies have dwindled and crushing plants will begin closing if Brazil does not import beans until its new crop is harvested next spring.
"They'll probably be looking at imports very quickly ... they're pretty much tapped out," said Mark Ash, trade analyst with USDA's Economic Research Service.

The USDA analysts said that Brazil is not yet officially on the books as having purchased any U.S. soybeans, but rumours circulated through the markets last week that U.S. soybean sales to unknown destinations during the week ending October 17 of 331,600 tonnes might be to Brazil.
Matthews noted that two years ago, Brazil ran short of soybeans and imported 1.2 million tonnes of soybeans, including 700,000 tonnes from the United States.

USDA is currently estimating Brazil to import a total 900,000 tonnes of soybean in 1996/97, up from last year's 600,000 tonnes. Most of Brazil's soybean imports normally come from Uruguay and Paraguay.

But come spring, analysts warned that with a good soybean crop and the recent elimination of export taxes on soybeans, Brazil will likely export more soybeans than normal and compete more aggressively with the United States.

Brazil has traditionally had higher export taxes on the raw soybean than the processed soybean meal and oil in order to encourage domestic crushing and the export of soyproducts. Analyst Ash said the new policy, along with a bigger crop, will now encourage more soybean exports.
Ash noted that soybean meal and oil exports will probably not decrease, but that because of expanded acreage and higher production, there will be enough soybeans left over to export.
"There will be plenty of crop for crushers. They'll be able to continue with a good pace of bean meal and oil exports," said Ash.

USDA is currently estimating Brazil soybean exports in 1996/97 to hit 3.5 million tonnes, up from last year's 3.2 million. Soybean meal exports are estimated at 11.40 million tonnes, versus 11.39 last year, and soyoil exports at 1.5 million tonnes, equal to last year's pace.
